item.title: The Mecca Pact could be an opportunity for Iran
item.description:
The Mecca Pact ranks among the most momentous developments to have reshaped the Middle East since the upheavals that followed the Hamas attacks on October 7, 2023.

Though defensive in nature, the agreement — which creates a mutual defense commitment between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey — could have major repercussions for the regional balance of power. Much hinges on how its signatories define the threats they must face and, more critically, on how other regional players, especially Iran and Israel, react to its creation.

Although the pact has come into being amid the ongoing U.S.‑Iran confrontation, it need not be construed as an expressly anti‑Iran coalition. On the contrary, Tehran has good reason to view it favorably.

The Turkish foreign minister indicated that preparations for the agreement had been underway for over two years. The Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA) between Riyadh and Islamabad was finalized within weeks of Israel’s attack on Qatar last year and may have been partially precipitated by it. Meanwhile, Egypt reportedly floated a proposal to establish a NATO‑style defense architecture in the region. Taken together, these developments suggest that Iran is not the target of the Mecca Pact.

This distinction matters in deciphering Iran’s position. One of the objectives underpinning Tehran’s war strategy was to demonstrate to regional states that an American military footprint could itself become a source of insecurity. Should Iran succeed in that aim, those governments are likely to pursue alternative security arrangements. Hence, the emergence of alternative regional defense frameworks would not necessarily signify a failure of Iranian strategy.

So far, Iran has expressed cautious optimism toward the pact. “Any plan that is based on the ⁠geopolitical and historical realities of the region, is comprehensive and inclusive, and correctly identifies the enemy ⁠and the threat, has a chance of helping to strengthen security ⁠and prevent instability and abuses by the Zionist enemy ⁠and its allies,” an Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson said last week.

Tehran has strong incentives to continue viewing the Mecca Pact with an open mind. The Mecca alliance has opened its doors to “all brotherly countries” seeking “lasting peace and stability,” meaning there is a possibility that Tehran could one day join the alliance.

This isn’t as much of a long shot as it might seem. After all, Iran has previously expressed openness to participating in the SMDA. If Tehran were prepared to enter into an alliance with Saudi Arabia, it would be all the less reluctant to do so when Turkey is also involved, given Ankara’s role in forestalling an Israel-backed Kurdish incursion into Iran this year.

Moreover, Turkey and Pakistan share deep historical, cultural, and religious ties with Iran. Iran’s broader regional narrative continues to resonate, to some degree, within their societies. These bonds do not erase differences but they suggest that neither country is likely to morph overnight into an implacable foe of Iran.

This leaves Iranian strategists with a clear choice. As it has done so far, Tehran should refrain from treating the pact as an anti‑Iran coalition. A pragmatic approach would keep alive the prospect of Iranian engagement with the emerging regional security architecture. Should U.S.‑Iranian diplomacy eventually yield a comprehensive nuclear agreement, many of the impediments to Iran’s participation in regional arrangements could also diminish.

The alternative would be to respond to the pact as an inherently anti‑Iran project, a reaction that risks turning into a self‑fulfilling prophecy. The alliance would then be compelled to organize its collective defense explicitly around the Iranian threat. Iran would also risk losing popular goodwill in the broader Muslim world. In this respect, strategic restraint may be Tehran’s best option.

The Israel factor


In practice, Iran may simply need to wait and see until time casts its spells.

After Hamas’s October 7 attack on southern Israel, Tel Aviv’s security doctrine acquired a somewhat peculiar pre‑emptive bent toward Ankara, with threats being tackled even before they had fully materialized. Since the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, for example, former Israeli officials have repeatedly labeled Turkey a “New Iran.” This narrative raises the prospect that regional strategic competition could gradually shift from an Israel‑Iran confrontation toward a more complex rivalry involving Israel and Turkey.

Furthermore, Turkey’s stake in Syria’s stability and Israel’s incursions into Syrian territory could eventually place them on a collision course. Israel’s insistence on maintaining “security zones” in various neighboring countries, including Lebanon, likewise betrays Tel Aviv’s reluctance to accommodate others. Over time, Israeli policies intended to forestall future threats could produce the opposite effect, spurring greater coordination among states constrained by Israeli power.

Iran stands to gain from this dynamic. Its existing regional network can no longer effectively counter Israeli influence. If a new regional arrangement gradually curbs Israel’s freedom of action, Tehran could secure additional strategic breathing room without having to confront Israel directly. It would thus appear to have a strong interest in allowing regional alignments to evolve.

The possible expansion of the Mecca Pact could reinforce this tendency. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has indicated that Egypt could join the agreement. Egypt’s history with Israel, combined with Turkey’s competing interests with Israel in the eastern Mediterranean, could eventually lead Israel to perceive an enlarged Mecca Pact as a mechanism of strategic containment. Such a perception would carry its own perils.

If Israel opts to counterbalance — as it is likely to do — both Israel and the bloc could fall victim to the security dilemma. Israel would seek more robust regional security partnerships, for instance with Somaliland and even with India, while members of the Mecca Pact might respond by further institutionalizing and expanding their collective defense arrangements.

From Tehran’s vantage point, such a development could offer opportunities. If Israel were forced to manage a broader array of regional rivalries, Iran would enjoy greater strategic space. The logic is not simply that the enemy of Iran’s enemy becomes its friend. Rather, a more complex regional equilibrium could reduce Israel’s capacity to concentrate its strategic resources on Iran and render accommodation with Tehran more appealing over time.

Nonetheless, the moment of truth may arrive much sooner.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia could eventually place Iran in direct tension with members of the Mecca Pact. Yet even here, neither side has an obvious incentive to put the alliance’s mutual‑defense commitment to the test. If Iran deliberately tested the pact by encouraging Houthi strikes, it could hasten the emergence of an explicitly anti‑Iran security posture. If Saudi Arabia invoked the pact in response to an attack, it could expose the alliance’s political limitations and reveal the thresholds for collective military action.

In fact, Pakistan and Turkey may encourage Saudi Arabia to exercise restraint. Both countries have demonstrated a preference for diplomatic management of regional crises. Their diplomacy played an important part in preventing Saudi Arabia from becoming a direct participant in the U.S.‑Iran conflict following Iranian attacks on Saudi facilities. Even under the SMDA framework, Pakistan did not automatically enter the war; instead, it emphasized de‑escalation. Their participation in the Mecca Pact could consequently introduce a diplomatic buffer rather than escalation.

This combination of deterrence and restraint could open up space for mutually acceptable arrangements on the Houthi question.

Even if Iran is bent on regional primacy, confrontation does not serve Iran’s interests. Iran may, therefore, have more reason to welcome the Mecca Pact than to fear it. What its strategists decide will shape the contours of the region’s future strategic environment.

item.title: An independent Europe means no more US rooster in the henhouse
item.description:
NATO continues to prepare for life without the United States, at least as the dominant alliance member. “Europeans are already backfilling what the U.S. cannot any longer promise,” explained Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

America's foreign policy establishmentarians have long worried about losing influence as a result. Indeed, by driving Europe away from America, Donald Trump may be inadvertently spurring creation of a serious counterweight to Washington. As CNN Fareed Zakaria warned: “As Europe’s spending increases, the continent will become less dependent on the U.S., and less deferential to it.”

American policymakers, he added, might therefore regret the disappearance of the continent as a military backwater governed by obsequious nonentities, which served as a convenient base for U.S. troops to operate around the globe.

The rise of Europe as an independent power will almost certainly transform international politics. And the process could be painful. One issue will be the difficulty of coordinating the militaries of more than a score of often dissonant perspectives within the European Union. Another is the return of Germany as a significant military power. Moreover, as European states increasingly talk about the possibility and, worse, likelihood, of war with Russia, Moscow may perceive a growing threat from the West and increase its military preparations accordingly.

However, the benefits for America will still far outweigh the problems.

Europeans’ reliance on Washington has long reduced their mutual cooperation. For instance, in 2020, years after Moscow wrested Crimea from Ukraine and backed separatists in the Donbas, the Pew Research Center asked Europeans if they favored defending their neighbors. Overall, sentiment was 50% to 38% against. Only in three of 13 countries polled did more people favor fighting for their supposed allies rather than standing by in case of war. In two, pluralities opposed doing so. A majority said no in eight, reaching 66% in Greece. Yet most Europeans still believed that America would intervene on their behalf.

This fecklessness encourages irresponsibility elsewhere. Last year the European Union surrendered economically, agreeing to President Donald Trump’s trade shakedown. EU policymakers and commentators claimed they had no choice, lest they be left to their own defense devices. For instance, European Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič observed: “It’s not only about … trade: It’s about security, it is about Ukraine, it is about current geopolitical volatility.”

And it’s about saving money; as Financial Times columnist Janan Ganesh asked: “How, if not through a smaller welfare state, is a better-armed continent to be funded?” Concern for such tradeoffs, until recently at least, trumped quaint concepts like sovereignty and self-respect. In this way, European subservience not only encouraged the administration’s irresponsible foreign policy, but also its modern, and destructive, mercantilist economic policy.

If the Europeans, and especially the EU, can no longer rely on Washington’s military umbrella, they will have to do more for their own security. This will place greater pressure on them to limit sclerotic rulemaking and liberalize existing controls. They will also have good reason to reject dubious and costly U.S. demands. And they will be more likely to confront American administrations directly when the next George W. Bush or Donald Trump decides to create another international disaster.

An equally important benefit would be to reduce America’s ability to meddle around the world, especially if a full U.S. military withdrawal from the continent ultimately results. Russia would no longer be viewed as a likely existential threat, at least in Washington, allowing the U.S. to follow by eliminating both its commitment to war and the force structure necessary to fulfill that obligation. Americans could then put these unlocked resources to better use elsewhere.

Thus, what some see as a likely problem would actually be an enormous advantage. True, Washington risks losing a subservient Europe willing to back its political interferences and serve as a launching pad for Washington’s military interventions. However, these policies have, more often than not, turned out disastrously. Even the globe’s nominally benign hegemon requires restraint.

The problem, as recognized by the historian John Dalberg-Acton, commonly known as Lord Acton, is that “power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.” That maxim applies even to the well-intentioned who wield overwhelming and largely unrestrained power. This includes the United States — especially when that nation is governed by a narcissist with spectacularly poor policy judgment.

Washington’s Cold War misjudgments were legendary. Vietnam was the worst but not alone. Seventy-three years on, supporting the coup that delivered absolute power to Mohammad Reza Pahlavi in Iran looks disastrous. Decisions like backing Pakistan’s Islamist government, headed by General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq, and funneling aid to Afghanistan’s Mujahedeen through later Pakistani regimes, which empowered the most radical insurgents, look terrible in light of 9/11 and succeeding developments.

However, such errors must be understood, if not excused, by the Cold War and competition with the Soviet Union. The latter was an Evil Empire like Ronald Reagan said, even if perhaps not as militarily aggressive as feared at the time. The same cannot be said for Washington’s missteps after the USSR’s collapse. “What we say goes,” announced President George H.W. Bush, when American policymakers really believed that the U.S. was the unipower and essential nation that could do no wrong.

Alas, hubris overwhelmed judgment, yielding the Somalia, Iraq, and Afghanistan debacles. After a quarter century of the “Global War on Terrorism,” nearly 5 million people have perished, most as an indirect result of the many conflicts. Few in Washington appeared to understand that wandering the globe bombing, invading, and occupying other nations, as well as backing other nations that did the same, would create enemies prepared to strike back with often terrible consequences.

Contra George W. Bush’s comfortable triumphalism, Americans were not attacked on 9/11 because they were so free and generous. Rather, a succession of administrations operating in their name spent years making other nations’ conflicts their own. Unfortunately, if you swat the hornet’s nest, you are likely to get stung.

The usual suspects in Washington tend to share Zakaria’s error in conflating their power to intervene internationally and Americans’ national interest. The former is often negative. Blob members typically enjoy running the world, or at least attempting to do so. Unfortunately, the rest of us pay the price.

If the president inadvertently strengthens Europe, so much the better for Americans as well as Europeans. U.S. policymakers have proved that their power, like that of adversary governments, require limits. A more powerful and dynamic Europe could help provide some.
